question.value: Search for cyanodiacetylene (HC5N) in Titan's atmosphere using ALMA archival data and constrain its abundance and photochemical models.

findings_qualitative.value: The upper limit [HC5N]/[HC3N] ratio on Titan derived for three of four models is lower than that measured in high-mass protostellar objects, implying less efficient synthesis of longer carbon chains on Titan, possibly due to lower C4H2 abundance.

evidence.quote: The corresponding upper limit of [HC 5 N]/[HC 3 N] ratio value derived from three of four models seem to be lower than that measured in high-mass protostellar objects, possibly due to the lower abundance of C 4 H 2 .

The relatively low [HC 5 N]/[HC 3 N] ratio we found implies that synthesis of progressively longer carbon chains is less efficient on Titan than in the cold interstellar medium and protostellar envelopes.

claims.hypothesis: HC5N emission lines (J = 96-95 and J = 99-98) can be detected in Titan's atmosphere by stacking deep archival ALMA Band 6 observations.
claims.experiment: Extracted and re-imaged six ALMA Band 6 execution blocks (total integration ~15,000 s) with a common 1.36 arcsec circular beam and 488 kHz resolution, and stacked the J = 96-95 and J = 99-98 transitions using noise-weighted averaging.
claims.result: No emission feature was detected at the HC5N rest frequency down to an rms noise level of 15 mK (~0.9 mJy beam^-1).
claims.finding: HC5N is not detected in Titan's atmosphere, setting a 3-sigma column density upper limit of 0.3–10 x 10^13 molecules cm^-2 above ~60 km (and a mixing ratio upper limit of 5.2 x 10^-11 in a two-layer model, 8 times lower than the previous Marten et al. 2002 limit).

evidence.quote: Integrating six independent observation data sets with a total integration time of ∼15,000 s, we found no statistically significant detection of an HC 5 N spectral feature.
The achieved noise level was measured to be as low as 15 mK in the brightness temperature scale, ∼0.9 mJy beam –1 in the flux density scale.

Our abundance upper limit of 5.2 × 10 −11 above 60 km is 8 times lower than the previously published upper limit for this species, which demonstrates the power of ALMA for searching for new molecules on Titan.

claims.hypothesis: Previously published photochemical models by Krasnopolsky (2009), Lellouch et al. (2010b), Loison et al. (2015), and Vuitton et al. (2019) accurately predict the vertical abundance of HC5N in Titan's atmosphere.
claims.experiment: Calculated synthetic spectra for all four vertical profiles using the Planetary Spectrum Generator (PSG) and determined the 3-sigma upper limit scaling factors against the stacked ALMA spectrum.
claims.result: The unscaled Lellouch et al. (2010b) and Krasnopolsky (2009) profiles predict peak intensities 47x and 23,000x the observed rms noise (3-sigma scaling factors of 0.074 and 0.00025), whereas the Vuitton et al. (2019) and Loison et al. (2015) profiles predict 0.63x and 0.03x the noise (3-sigma scaling factors of 5.1 and 21.6).
claims.finding: The nondetection rules out the Lellouch et al. (2010b) and Krasnopolsky (2009) models as overestimates, while remaining consistent with the lower abundances predicted by Loison et al. (2015) and Vuitton et al. (2019).

claims.hypothesis: The [HC5N]/[HC3N] abundance ratio in Titan's atmosphere is comparable to that observed in high-mass protostellar objects (HMPOs, average 0.29).
claims.experiment: Compared the 3-sigma HC5N column density upper limits above 60 km to the ALMA-derived HC3N column density above 60 km (2.3 x 10^14 molecules cm^-2 from Cordiner et al. 2014).
claims.result: The upper limit [HC5N]/[HC3N] ratio above 60 km is 0.012–0.17 for three of the four models and <0.43 for the Vuitton et al. (2019) model.
claims.finding: The [HC5N]/[HC3N] ratio on Titan appears lower than or at most comparable to HMPOs, indicating less efficient synthesis of longer carbon chains on Titan, likely due to lower C4H2 abundance.

The relatively low [HC 5 N]/[HC 3 N] ratio we found implies that synthesis of progressively longer carbon chains is less efficient on Titan than in the cold interstellar medium and protostellar envelopes.

why_this_data.value: Project 2019.1.00783.S covered several HC5N transitions and had long integration times (2000–3000 s per execution), providing the highest achievable sensitivity ever for Titan in this frequency range.

evidence.quote: We found out the data sets also include several HC 5 N transitions. In addition, since the integration time of each measurement was long (2000–3000 s), achievable total sensitivity was the highest ever for Titan, in this frequency range.

why_this_method.value: Spectral stacking integrates multiple observations and transitions to improve sensitivity to weak emission lines; re-CLEANing to a common 1.36 arcsec circular beam and smoothing to 488 kHz accounts for differing native spatial and spectral resolutions across the six datasets.

evidence.quote: To identify the weak HC 5 N emission line, the spectral stacking technique (e.g., L. Neumann et al. 2023), which integrates multiple spectra acquired in different measurements, was employed.
